104
BIOLOGY
There is a wide diversity in living organisms in our biosphere. Now a
question that arises in our minds is: Are all living organisms made of the
same chemicals, i.e., elements and compounds? You have learnt in
chemistry how elemental analysis is performed. If we perform such an
analysis on a plant tissue, animal tissue or a microbial paste, we obtain a

Now a question that arises in our minds is: Are all living organisms made of the same chemicals, i.e., elements and compounds?

activities.subject: Biology
activities.question: Compare two important ideas from Chapter 9.
activities.instructions: Use the source-based options to complete this activity.

correctItems.text: In absolute terms, no such differences could be made out.
All the elements present in a sample of earth's crust are also present in a sample of living tissue.
However, a closer examination reveals that the relative abundance of carbon and hydrogen with respect to other elements is higher in any living organism than in earth's crust (Table 9.1).
We can continue asking in the same way, what type of organic compounds are found in living organisms?

activities.question: Connect causes and effects from Chapter 9.
activities.instructions: Use the source-based options to complete this activity.

correctItems.text: To get an answer, one has to perform a chemical analysis.
We can take any living tissue (a vegetable or a piece of liver, etc.) and grind it in trichloroacetic acid (Cl3CCOOH) using a mortar and a pestle.
If we were to strain this through a cheesecloth or cotton we would obtain two fractions.
One is called the filtrate or more technically, the acid-soluble pool, and the second, the retentate or the acid-insoluble fraction.

activities.subject: Biology
activities.question: Arrange key steps or ideas from Chapter 9 in order.
activities.instructions: Use the source-based options to complete this activity.

correctItems.text: Scientists have found thousands of organic compounds in the acid-soluble pool.
It will suffice to say here that one extracts the compounds, then subjects the extract to various separation techniques till one has separated a compound from all other compounds.
Analytical techniques, when applied to the compound give us an idea of the molecular formula and the probable structure of the compound.
All the carbon compounds that we get from living tissues can be called 'biomolecules'.

One weighs a small amount of a living tissue (say a leaf or liver and this is called wet weight) and dry it.
Now if the tissue is fully burnt, all the carbon compounds are oxidised to gaseous form (CO2, water vapour) and are removed.

Now if the tissue is fully burnt, all the carbon compounds are oxidised to gaseous form (CO2, water vapour) and are removed.
